references.text: Matthew's parallel account of the synagogue ruler (Jairus) who comes to Jesus, falls down before him, and asks him to come to his house because his daughter is dead/dying.
Mark's parallel account of Jairus, one of the synagogue rulers, who falls at Jesus' feet and earnestly begs him to come and lay hands on his dying daughter.

Crispus, the synagogue ruler in Corinth, is mentioned as one who believed in the Lord. Jairus was also a synagogue ruler (ἄρχων τῆς συναγωγῆς), showing that some leaders of the synagogue came to faith.
The synagogue rulers in Antioch of Pisidia are mentioned, highlighting the role of synagogue ruler (ἀρχισυνάγωγοι)—the same position Jairus held.
A leper falls on his face before Jesus and asks him for healing, similarly to how Jairus falls at Jesus' feet and earnestly begs him.
An officer (centurion) sends messengers to Jesus and asks him to come to his house to heal a servant who is dying. A parallel to Jairus asking Jesus to come to his home to heal his dying daughter.
The continuation of Mark's parallel account where Jesus goes to Jairus' house and raises his daughter from the dead.
The verse that immediately follows explains why Jairus was so desperate: he had only one daughter, about twelve years old, and she was at the point of death.
The synagogue ruler in this text reacts negatively to Jesus' healing on the Sabbath, in contrast to Jairus who himself seeks out Jesus and asks for healing.
